summary: In part 96 of his mini-series on stimulating ecstatic love for Krishna, Indradyumna Swami continues examining Krishna's first transcendental quality—that He performs wonderful varieties of pastimes—focusing on His childhood lila as relished by the elder gopis of Vrindavan. Drawing extensively on Srila Jiva Goswami's Gopala-campu, he explains how the different phases of Krishna's pastimes (birth and infancy witnessed by the elders of Braja, boyhood victories over demigods seen by His young friends, His mercy to Kaliya and other demons seen by the devotees, and His love pastimes with the gopis) are all glorified in song, and that this Vraja-prema is beyond logic and cannot be dissected by reason. Jiva Goswami further teaches that there is no real difference between Krishna's 'happy' and 'sad' pastimes—they are as inseparable as milk mixed with water—and that all five rasas (santa, dasya, sakhya, vatsalya, madhurya) are woven together in them, illustrated by tender exchanges between baby Krishna, Mother Yasoda, and Nanda Maharaja. The Swami then recounts Surdas's very first poem, recited before his guru Vallabhacharya at Mathura, describing the ocean of bliss (ananda-sagara) that flooded Braja at Krishna's birth: gopis rushing to Nanda's home fully decorated like caged birds freed after ages, their flowers raining down, cows running mad with ecstasy, and Nanda giving cows and charity to the brahmanas—a recitation so ecstatic that Surdas's voice choked and Vallabhacharya had to complete the final Brajbhasha stanza. He adds Parmananda Das's account of the sages Garga, Sandila, Bhrigu, and Agastya coming the next day to bless Yasoda, marveling that the infinite Lord who reclines on the milk ocean stayed in her small womb, and Kaviratna's verse that one who daily sings the glories of Yasoda's son is never troubled by Kali-yuga. Summarizing a week of his own reading, he shares intimate vignettes: baby Krishna and Balarama clothed only by the ten directions with waist-bells and anklets as their sole ornaments; Yasoda repeatedly dressing Krishna as a prince only for Him to strip off every ornament and dhoti, keeping just a peacock feather; His possessiveness over toys and tantrums; His clapping and dancing ('ti-ti, ti-ti') to the gopis' singing with skill mysterious even to Lord Shiva; and His stumbling, then running to hide under His mother's veil to drink her breast milk. He closes with a prayer from Rupa Goswami's Padyavali longing for the vision of infant Krishna decorated with a peacock feather, nursing at His mother's breast, to enter the pathway of one's eyes.
key_points: This is part 96 of a series on stimulating ecstatic love, treating Krishna's quality of performing wonderful pastimes—here His childhood lila, mainly relished by the elder gopis of Vrindavan.

From Jiva Goswami's Gopala-campu: Krishna's pastimes (birth/infancy, boyhood victories, mercy to demons, love with gopis) are all glorified in song, and Vraja-prema is beyond logic and cannot be understood by reasoning.
There is no difference between Krishna's happy and sad pastimes—inseparable like milk and water—and all five rasas (santa, dasya, sakhya, vatsalya, madhurya) are blended within them.
Krishna's childhood pastimes are called ananda-sagara, an 'ocean of bliss,' which inundated Braja at His birth in the home of Nanda and Yasoda.

Surdas's first poem—recited before his guru Vallabhacharya at Mathura—vividly describes decorated gopis rushing to Nanda's home like freed caged birds, ecstatic cows, and Nanda's charity; Surdas choked with emotion and Vallabhacharya finished the final stanza.

Intimate vignettes: Yasoda repeatedly dresses Krishna as a prince but He strips off everything except a peacock feather; He is possessive of toys, steals Balarama's, and throws tantrums; He dances and claps ('ti-ti') to the gopis' songs with skill mysterious even to Lord Shiva.
When Krishna stumbles He runs to hide under Yasoda's veil and nurse; a jealous Balarama does likewise, and the two brothers fall asleep—followed by a closing prayer from Rupa Goswami's Padyavali.
references: Gopala-campu (Purva-campu / Prathama Puranam) by Srila Jiva Goswami — primary source for the lecture; speaker cites verse 142 on Krishna's pastimes being glorified in song and that Vraja-prema is beyond logic ('That love will not tolerate the logician's attempts to discuss and understand it').

Gopala-campu, Jiva Goswami — statement that happy and sad pastimes cannot be separated, 'Can anyone separate milk and water when they are mixed together?', naming the five rasas: santa, dasya, sakhya, vatsalya, madhurya.

Gopala-campu, Jiva Goswami — the two verses of tender exchange: Krishna, 'Mother! Mother! Give it to me!' and Yasoda, 'O my child! My calf! My boy!'; plus Nanda Maharaja's words to Yasoda, 'You must have performed many pious deeds in past lives.'

Surdas — his first poem describing Krishna's appearance in the home of Nanda and Yasoda (in Brajbhasha), recited before his guru Vallabhacharya (Ballabhacharya) at Mathura; final stanza completed by Vallabhacharya beginning 'Te din ve log...' ('From that day on, the residents of Braj were never lacking pleasure...').

Parmananda Das — poem on the sages Garga, Sandila, Bhrigu, and Agastya visiting the day after Krishna's birth to bless Yasoda, wondering how the Lord 'who sleeps on the waters of the milk ocean' stayed in her small womb.

Shri Kaviratna — verse (attributed to Rupa Goswami's Padyavali) that one who daily sings the glories of Yasoda's son 'is never troubled by Kali-yuga' but finds 'a torrential flood of the sweetest nectar.'

Rupa Goswami's Padyavali — closing prayer: 'When will infant Krishna, charmingly decorated with a large peacock feather on his head, wriggling his lotus toes, his lotus mouth placed on his mother's breast, enter the pathway of my eyes?'
stories: Milk and water mixed — Jiva Goswami's image that Krishna's 'happy' and 'sad' pastimes can no more be separated than milk blended with water.
Surdas's first poem — the poet recited his maiden verse on Krishna's birth before his guru Vallabhacharya at Mathura, but choked with ecstasy, so the guru completed the final Brajbhasha stanza.
Gopis like caged birds set free — hearing of Krishna's birth, decorated gopis rushed to Nanda's home like birds freed after ages of captivity, their flowers raining down from loosened braids.
Yasoda dressing Krishna as a prince — she ties a golden dhoti and hangs necklaces on Him, but He strips off every ornament, keeping only a peacock feather as His crown.
Krishna dancing 'ti-ti, ti-ti' — to distract His roving eyes the gopis ask Him to dance, and He claps and recites playful sounds while skillfully moving in time to their singing.
Krishna's tantrums and thefts — He flies into a rage if His smallest toy is taken, yet laughs and refuses to return Balarama's toys, scheming to steal them again.
Stumbling into mother's veil — when He falls mid-dance Krishna runs to hide under Yasoda's veil and nurse contentedly; a jealous Balarama does the same, and the brothers fall asleep.
quotes: I hope someday I will love Krishna as they do, and so do we.
That love will not tolerate the logician's attempts to discuss and understand it.
The whole of Braj was shaking in bliss.
But as soon as she finished, Krishna would undo all her hard work.
